title: Πατρόκλου ψυχή
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The Achaeans scatter to their ships, but Achilles keeps the Myrmidons together and has them drive their horses three times round Patroclus’ body, lamenting; he lays his hands on his friend’s chest and promises Hector dragged to the dogs and twelve Trojan captives at the pyre. Funeral feasting follows, with beasts slaughtered by the hundred. The kings bring Achilles to Agamemnon, but he refuses to wash off the blood until Patroclus is burned and buried, and asks that wood be fetched at dawn. After the meal he lies down on the shore and sleeps, and the ghost of Patroclus stands over him, begging for burial so that he may cross into Hades, and asking that their bones lie together in the golden jar. Achilles promises to do it all and asks him to come close so that they may mourn once more.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἳ μὲν στενάχοντο κατὰ πτόλιν· αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὶ
ἐπεὶ δὴ νῆάς τε καὶ Ἑλλήσποντον ἵκοντο,
sentences.tr:
hōs hoi men stenachonto kata ptolin· autar Achaioi
epei dē nēas te kai Hellēsponton hikonto,
sentences.l:
So they groaned throughout the city; but the Achaeans,
when they had come to the ships and the Hellespont,
sentences.i: So they groaned throughout the city; but the Achaeans, when they had come to the ships and the Hellespont,
sentences.n: The first line closes the Trojan lament of Book 22: ὣς οἳ μὲν στενάχοντο ‘so they groaned’, the Trojans in the city, set against αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοί ‘but the Achaeans’. The clause ἐπεὶ δὴ … ἵκοντο ‘when they had come’ (aorist of ἱκνέομαι) has νῆάς ‘ships’ and the Hellespont as its goal, and the main verb comes only in the next unit. Line 2 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the opening syllable of ἐπεί, short by nature, has to count long.

sentences.t: οἳ μὲν ἄρ’ ἐσκίδναντο ἑὴν ἐπὶ νῆα ἕκαστος,
sentences.tr: hoi men ar’ eskidnanto heēn epi nēa hekastos,
sentences.l: They, then, scattered, each to his own ship,
sentences.i: They scattered, each to his own ship,
sentences.n: οἳ μὲν ἄρ’ is ‘they, then’, the army at large as against the Myrmidons of the next line. ἐσκίδναντο is the imperfect of σκίδναμαι ‘scatter’, ἑὴν is the epic form of ἣν ‘his own’, and νῆα is the old accusative singular of ‘ship’. The line stands in iliad-125 with the same English.

sentences.t:
Μυρμιδόνας δ’ οὐκ εἴα ἀποσκίδνασθαι Ἀχιλλεύς,
ἀλλ’ ὅ γε οἷς ἑτάροισι φιλοπτολέμοισι μετηύδα·
sentences.tr:
Myrmidonas d’ ouk eia aposkidnasthai Achilleus,
all’ ho ge hois hetaroisi philoptolemoisi metēuda·
sentences.l:
but the Myrmidons Achilles did not allow to scatter,
but he to his own war-loving companions spoke among them:
sentences.i: but Achilles would not let the Myrmidons scatter; he spoke among his own war-loving companions:
sentences.n: οὐκ εἴα is the imperfect of ἐάω ‘allow’, with ἀποσκίδνασθαι ‘to scatter’ as its infinitive. Μυρμιδόνας is the accusative object, and Achilles’ own companions (οἷς ἑτάροισι) are the Myrmidons again. φιλοπτολέμοισι is ‘war-loving’, and μετηύδα, from μεταυδάω, is ‘spoke among them’; the colon opens his speech.

sentences.t:
Μυρμιδόνες ταχύπωλοι ἐμοὶ ἐρίηρες ἑταῖροι
μὴ δή πω ὑπ’ ὄχεσφι λυώμεθα μώνυχας ἵππους,
sentences.tr:
Myrmidones tachypōloi emoi eriēres hetairoi
mē dē pō hyp’ ochesphi lyōmetha mōnychas hippous,
sentences.l:
“Myrmidons swift-colted, my trusty companions,
let us not yet loose from the chariots the solid-hoofed horses,
sentences.i: “Myrmidons with your swift colts, my trusty companions, let us not yet unyoke the solid-hoofed horses from the chariots,
sentences.n: Achilles is speaking, and he addresses his own men. ταχύπωλοι is ‘swift-colted’ (πῶλος ‘colt, foal’), and ἐρίηρες ἑταῖροι ‘trusty companions’, the sense of ἐρίηρος not being fully known. μὴ δή πω … λυώμεθα is a prohibition in the subjunctive, ‘let us not yet loose’; ὑπ’ ὄχεσφι is ‘from beneath the chariots’ (ὄχεσφι with the ending -φι), and μώνυχας ‘solid-hoofed’ means having an undivided hoof.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ αὐτοῖς ἵπποισι καὶ ἅρμασιν ἆσσον ἰόντες
Πάτροκλον κλαίωμεν· ὃ γὰρ γέρας ἐστὶ θανόντων.
sentences.tr:
all’ autois hippoisi kai harmasin asson iontes
Patroklon klaiōmen· ho gar geras esti thanontōn.
sentences.l:
but with the horses themselves and the chariots, going close,
let us mourn Patroclus; for that is the prize of the dead.
sentences.i: but let us drive close with horses and chariots as they are and mourn Patroclus; for that is the prize of honour that belongs to the dead.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ αὐτοῖς ἵπποισι καὶ ἅρμασιν is ‘but with the very horses and chariots’, still harnessed, and ἆσσον ἰόντες ‘going nearer’ brings them up to the body. κλαίωμεν is a subjunctive of exhortation, ‘let us mourn’. γέρας ‘prize, prize of honour’ is what the dead are owed, and ὃ γάρ gives the reason.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί κ’ ὀλοοῖο τεταρπώμεσθα γόοιο,
ἵππους λυσάμενοι δορπήσομεν ἐνθάδε πάντες.
sentences.tr:
autar epei k’ olooio tetarpōmestha gooio,
hippous lysamenoi dorpēsomen enthade pantes.
sentences.l:
But when we have taken our fill of baneful lament,
having loosed the horses, we shall take supper here, all of us.”
sentences.i: But when we have taken our fill of baneful lament, we shall unyoke the horses and all take supper here.”
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεί κ’ is ‘but when’, with κε and the aorist subjunctive τεταρπώμεσθα (from τέρπομαι, here ‘take one’s fill of’, with the genitive γόοιο ‘lament’). ὀλοοῖο is ‘baneful’. λυσάμενοι ‘having loosed’ is the aorist middle participle, and δορπήσομεν the future of δορπέω ‘take supper’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ᾤμωξαν ἀολλέες, ἦρχε δ’ Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ōimōxan aollees, ērche d’ Achilleus.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they wailed in a close mass, and Achilles led.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they cried out in a close mass, with Achilles leading.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘so he spoke’ (ἔφαθ’ for ἔφατο). ᾤμωξαν is the aorist of οἰμώζω ‘wail’, which i gives as ‘cried out’, and ἀολλέες means ‘in a close mass’. ἦρχε δ’ Ἀχιλλεύς is ‘and Achilles led’, as the one who leads off a lament does.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ τρὶς περὶ νεκρὸν ἐΰτριχας ἤλασαν ἵππους
μυρόμενοι·
sentences.tr:
hoi de tris peri nekron eÿtrichas ēlasan hippous
myromenoi·
sentences.l:
And they three times around the corpse drove the well-maned horses,
mourning;
sentences.i: Three times they drove the well-maned horses round the corpse, mourning;
sentences.n: ἤλασαν is the aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, with ἵππους as object, and τρίς ‘three times’ marks a rite. ἐΰτριχας ‘well-maned’ is ἐΰ ‘well’ and θρίξ ‘hair’, and the edition prints the diaeresis. μυρόμενοι ‘mourning’ is a present participle, and the stop after it closes the unit.

sentences.t: μετὰ δέ σφι Θέτις γόου ἵμερον ὦρσε.
sentences.tr: meta de sphi Thetis goou himeron ōrse.
sentences.l: and among them Thetis roused the longing for lament.
sentences.i: and among them Thetis roused the longing to lament.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 14. μετὰ … σφι is ‘among them’, the preposition μετά with its dative pronoun and the particle δέ between them, and ἵμερον ‘longing’ is the object of ὦρσε, the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’. The poet does not show Thetis; she is the mother of Achilles, who stirs the mourners’ grief, in a way he leaves unexplained.

sentences.t:
δεύοντο ψάμαθοι, δεύοντο δὲ τεύχεα φωτῶν
δάκρυσι· τοῖον γὰρ πόθεον μήστωρα φόβοιο.
sentences.tr:
deuonto psamathoi, deuonto de teuchea phōtōn
dakrysi· toion gar potheon mēstōra phoboio.
sentences.l:
Wet were the sands, wet too the armour of the men
with tears; for such a man they longed for, master of flight.
sentences.i: The sands were wet, and the men’s armour was wet, with tears; for they missed such a man, a master of flight.
sentences.n: δεύοντο is the imperfect passive of δεύω ‘wet’, repeated in the second half of the line (δεύοντο δὲ), and δάκρυσι ‘with tears’ completes both halves. τεύχεα is ‘armour’ and φωτῶν ‘of men’. τοῖον … μήστωρα φόβοιο is ‘such a master of flight’, a man who could rout the enemy; πόθεον is the imperfect of ποθέω ‘long for’, which i gives as ‘missed’.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δὲ Πηλεΐδης ἁδινοῦ ἐξῆρχε γόοιο
χεῖρας ἐπ’ ἀνδροφόνους θέμενος στήθεσσιν ἑταίρου·
sentences.tr:
toisi de Pēleïdēs hadinou exērche gooio
cheiras ep’ androphonous themenos stēthessin hetairou·
sentences.l:
And among them Peleus’-son led off the thronging lament,
laying his man-slaying hands on the breast of his companion,
sentences.i: Among them the son of Peleus led off the thronging lament, laying his man-slaying hands on his companion’s breast,
sentences.n: Πηλεΐδης is ‘son of Peleus’, Achilles. ἐξῆρχε is the imperfect of ἐξάρχω ‘lead off’, with the genitive ἁδινοῦ γόοιο ‘the thronging lament’. χεῖρας ἐπ’ ἀνδροφόνους θέμενος is ‘having laid his man-slaying hands on’, and στήθεσσιν ‘the breast’ is the epic dative plural. The first two lines stand also in iliad-119, with the same English, which ends in a comma; here the Greek ends in a high stop and his speech follows in the next unit.

sentences.t: χαῖρέ μοι ὦ Πάτροκλε καὶ εἰν Ἀΐδαο δόμοισι·
sentences.tr: chaire moi ō Patrokle kai ein Aïdao domoisi·
sentences.l: “Be glad, Patroclus, even in the houses of Hades;
sentences.i: “Be glad, Patroclus, even in the house of Hades;
sentences.n: Achilles speaks to the dead man. χαῖρε is ‘be glad’, with μοι a dative of the speaker’s concern that the English leaves out; the words are a greeting that is also a farewell. καὶ εἰν Ἀΐδαο δόμοισι is ‘even in the houses of Hades’, the plural δόμοισι being the epic dative, and the Ἀΐδαο is the genitive of Ἅιδης, whose diaeresis is printed.

sentences.t:
πάντα γὰρ ἤδη τοι τελέω τὰ πάροιθεν ὑπέστην
Ἕκτορα δεῦρ’ ἐρύσας δώσειν κυσὶν ὠμὰ δάσασθαι,
sentences.tr:
panta gar ēdē toi teleō ta paroithen hypestēn
Hektora deur’ erysas dōsein kysin ōma dasasthai,
sentences.l:
for all things now I am fulfilling for you that I undertook before,
that I would drag Hector here and give him to dogs to tear raw,
sentences.i: for now I am fulfilling for you everything I undertook before: to drag Hector here and give him raw to the dogs to tear,
sentences.n: τελέω is ‘I am fulfilling’, with πάντα … τὰ πάροιθεν ὑπέστην ‘all that I undertook before’ (ὑπέστην, aorist of ὑφίσταμαι); τοι is ‘to you’. What he undertook is given in the future infinitive δώσειν ‘to give’, with ἐρύσας ‘having dragged’ (an aorist participle) before it; ὠμά is ‘raw’ (the flesh), and δάσασθαι ‘to tear apart, share out’ is the aorist infinitive of δατέομαι.

sentences.t:
δώδεκα δὲ προπάροιθε πυρῆς ἀποδειροτομήσειν
Τρώων ἀγλαὰ τέκνα σέθεν κταμένοιο χολωθείς.
sentences.tr:
dōdeka de proparoithe pyrēs apodeirotomēsein
Trōōn aglaa tekna sethen ktamenoio cholōtheis.
sentences.l:
and twelve, before the pyre, to cut the throats of,
the splendid children of the Trojans, angered at your being slain.”
sentences.i: and, before the pyre, to cut the throats of twelve splendid children of the Trojans, in anger at your being slain.”
sentences.n: The infinitive ἀποδειροτομήσειν ‘to cut the throats of’ (ἀπο- + δειρή ‘neck’ + τέμνω) runs on from δώσειν in the last unit, still depending on ὑπέστην. The twelve are Τρώων ἀγλαὰ τέκνα ‘the splendid children of the Trojans’, and σέθεν κταμένοιο is ‘of you slain’ (σέθεν the epic genitive of σύ; κταμένοιο aorist participle of κτείνω), so χολωθείς ‘angered’ is for his friend’s death. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα καὶ Ἕκτορα δῖον ἀεικέα μήδετο ἔργα
πρηνέα πὰρ λεχέεσσι Μενοιτιάδαο τανύσσας
ἐν κονίῃς·
sentences.tr:
ē rha kai Hektora dion aeikea mēdeto erga
prēnea par lecheessi Menoitiadao tanyssas
en koniēis·
sentences.i: So he said, and planned unseemly deeds against heavenly Hector, stretching him face down beside the bier of Menoetius’ son in the dust;
sentences.n: A new paragraph. ἦ ῥα is ‘so he spoke’, a formula that closes a speech, here followed by the narrator’s turn to what Achilles does. Ἕκτορα δῖον is ‘heavenly Hector’ and ἀεικέα … ἔργα ‘unseemly deeds’, planned by μήδετο (imperfect of μήδομαι). πρηνέα ‘face down’ agrees with Ἕκτορα, τανύσσας ‘having stretched’ is the aorist participle, and Μενοιτιάδαο is the patronymic ‘son of Menoetius’, Patroclus; λεχέεσσι, a plural in form, is the one bier (λέχος is properly ‘bed’). The first line stands in iliad-141 with the same English.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἔντε’ ἀφωπλίζοντο ἕκαστος
χάλκεα μαρμαίροντα, λύον δ’ ὑψηχέας ἵππους,
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ ente’ aphōplizonto hekastos
chalkea marmaironta, lyon d’ hypsēcheas hippous,
sentences.l:
and they each took off their armour,
bronze, sparkling, and loosed the high-sounding horses,
sentences.i: and the men each took off their sparkling bronze armour and unyoked the high-sounding horses,
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 26. ἔντε’ is ἔντεα ‘gear, armour’, and ἀφωπλίζοντο (imperfect middle of ἀφοπλίζομαι) is ‘took off their arms’. χάλκεα μαρμαίροντα is ‘bronze, sparkling’, and ὑψηχέας ‘high-sounding’ (ὕψι ‘high’ and ἠχέω ‘sound’) probably describes the horses’ neighing; the sense is not certain.

sentences.t:
κὰδ δ’ ἷζον παρὰ νηῒ ποδώκεος Αἰακίδαο
μυρίοι·
sentences.tr:
kad d’ hizon para nēï podōkeos Aiakidao
myrioi·
sentences.l:
and sat down beside the ship of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus,
countless;
sentences.i: and sat down in their countless numbers beside the ship of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus;
sentences.n: κὰδ … ἷζον is ‘sat down’ (κατά in tmesis, with its final consonant assimilated to the δ that follows; ἷζον the imperfect of ἵζω). ποδώκεος Αἰακίδαο is ‘of the fleet-footed descendant of Aeacus’, which is Achilles, grandson of Aeacus through Peleus. μυρίοι is ‘countless’, and the stop after it closes the unit.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὃ τοῖσι τάφον μενοεικέα δαίνυ.
sentences.tr: autar ho toisi taphon menoeikea dainy.
sentences.l: but he for them a satisfying funeral feast was giving.
sentences.i: and he gave them a satisfying funeral feast.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 29. αὐτὰρ ὅ is ‘but he’, Achilles again, and τοῖσι ‘for them’. τάφον is ‘funeral feast’, the meal that goes with burial, and δαίνυ is the imperfect of δαίνυμι ‘give a feast’. μενοεικέα is ‘satisfying’, literally ‘to the heart’s liking’.

sentences.t:
πολλοὶ μὲν βόες ἀργοὶ ὀρέχθεον ἀμφὶ σιδήρῳ
σφαζόμενοι, πολλοὶ δ’ ὄϊες καὶ μηκάδες αἶγες·
sentences.tr:
polloi men boes argoi orechtheon amphi sidērōi
sphazomenoi, polloi d’ oïes kai mēkades aiges·
sentences.l:
Many white oxen bellowed around the iron,
being slaughtered, and many sheep and bleating goats;
sentences.i: Many white oxen bellowed round the knife as they were slaughtered, and many sheep and bleating goats;
sentences.n: ὀρέχθεον is the imperfect of ὀρεχθέω ‘bellow’, and ἀμφὶ σιδήρῳ is ‘around the iron’, the blade that kills them, so i says ‘knife’. βόες ἀργοί is ‘white oxen’; ἀργός means ‘gleaming white’ here, and ‘swift’ elsewhere in the poems. μηκάδες is ‘bleating’, from μηκάομαι, and ὄϊες ‘sheep’; σφαζόμενοι ‘being slaughtered’ is a passive participle.

sentences.t:
πολλοὶ δ’ ἀργιόδοντες ὕες θαλέθοντες ἀλοιφῇ
εὑόμενοι τανύοντο διὰ φλογὸς Ἡφαίστοιο·
sentences.tr:
polloi d’ argiodontes hyes thalethontes aloiphēi
heuomenoi tanyonto dia phlogos Hēphaistoio·
sentences.l:
and many white-toothed pigs, abundant with fat,
being singed, were stretched out through the flame of Hephaestus;
sentences.i: and many white-toothed pigs, abounding in fat, were stretched out to be singed through the flame of Hephaestus;
sentences.n: ἀργιόδοντες ‘white-toothed’ describes pigs with gleaming tusks, and ὕες is ‘pigs’. θαλέθοντες ἀλοιφῇ is ‘abounding in fat’ (θαλέθω ‘thrive’, ἀλοιφή ‘fat’). εὑόμενοι ‘being singed’ is a passive participle of εὕω, and τανύοντο ‘were stretched out’ is the imperfect passive; Ἡφαίστοιο ‘of Hephaestus’ stands for fire. Line 33 stands in iliad-056 in the same words, and its English is reused.

sentences.t: πάντῃ δ’ ἀμφὶ νέκυν κοτυλήρυτον ἔρρεεν αἷμα.
sentences.tr: pantēi d’ amphi nekyn kotylēryton erreen haima.
sentences.l: and everywhere about the corpse in cupfuls ran the blood.
sentences.i: and all round the corpse the blood ran in cupfuls.
sentences.n: πάντῃ ἀμφὶ νέκυν is ‘everywhere around the corpse’, Patroclus’ body on its bier. ἔρρεεν is the imperfect of ῥέω ‘flow’, and κοτυλήρυτον is ‘in cupfuls’, blood flowing so plentifully that it could be drawn off in cups (κοτύλη ‘small cup’); the second part of the word is from ἀρύω ‘draw’ or ῥέω ‘flow’, which is not certain.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ τόν γε ἄνακτα ποδώκεα Πηλεΐωνα
εἰς Ἀγαμέμνονα δῖον ἄγον βασιλῆες Ἀχαιῶν
σπουδῇ παρπεπιθόντες ἑταίρου χωόμενον κῆρ.
sentences.tr:
autar ton ge anakta podōkea Pēleïōna
eis Agamemnona dion agon basilēes Achaiōn
spoudēi parpepithontes hetairou chōomenon kēr.
sentences.l:
But him, the lord, the fleet-footed son of Peleus,
to Agamemnon the heavenly the kings of the Achaeans led,
with effort persuading him, incensed at heart for his companion.
sentences.i: But the kings of the Achaeans led the lord, the fleet-footed son of Peleus, to heavenly Agamemnon, having persuaded him with effort, for his heart was incensed over his companion.
sentences.n: A new paragraph, with the object put first: τόν γε ἄνακτα ποδώκεα Πηλεΐωνα is ‘him, the lord, the fleet-footed son of Peleus’, Achilles, and βασιλῆες Ἀχαιῶν the subject. ἄγον is the imperfect of ἄγω ‘lead’. σπουδῇ παρπεπιθόντες is ‘having persuaded him with effort’ (παρπεπιθόντες is the aorist participle of παραπείθω, with the doubling of the root). χωόμενον κῆρ is ‘incensed at heart’, and ἑταίρου ‘for his companion’ gives the cause.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ κλισίην Ἀγαμέμνονος ἷξον ἰόντες,
sentences.tr: hoi d’ hote dē klisiēn Agamemnonos hixon iontes,
sentences.l: And when they came, going, to Agamemnon’s hut,
sentences.i: When they had come to Agamemnon’s hut,
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ is ‘and when’, the kings and Achilles. ἷξον is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘come’, with κλισίην ‘hut’, and ἰόντες ‘going’ is a participle that adds only the sense of movement.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα κηρύκεσσι λιγυφθόγγοισι κέλευσαν
ἀμφὶ πυρὶ στῆσαι τρίποδα μέγαν, εἰ πεπίθοιεν
Πηλεΐδην λούσασθαι ἄπο βρότον αἱματόεντα.
sentences.tr:
autika kērykessi ligyphthongoisi keleusan
amphi pyri stēsai tripoda megan, ei pepithoien
Pēleïdēn lousasthai apo broton haimatoenta.
sentences.l:
at once to the clear-voiced heralds they gave command
to set a great tripod about the fire, if they might persuade
Peleus’-son to wash off the bloody gore.
sentences.i: they at once told the clear-voiced heralds to set a great tripod over the fire, in case they could persuade the son of Peleus to wash the bloody gore from himself.
sentences.n: κηρύκεσσι λιγυφθόγγοισι is ‘the clear-voiced heralds’, and κέλευσαν ‘gave command’ takes the infinitive στῆσαι ‘to set’; the tripod is a cauldron for heating the bath water. εἰ πεπίθοιεν is ‘if they might persuade’, an optative that gives the hope behind the order. λούσασθαι ἄπο is ‘to wash off’ (ἄπο after its verb), βρότον ‘gore’ is clotted blood, and αἱματόεντα ‘bloody’ agrees with it.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἠρνεῖτο στερεῶς, ἐπὶ δ’ ὅρκον ὄμοσσεν·
sentences.tr: autar ho g’ ērneito stereōs, epi d’ horkon omossen·
sentences.l: But he refused firmly, and besides swore an oath:
sentences.i: But he firmly refused, and swore an oath to it:
sentences.n: ἠρνεῖτο is the imperfect of ἀρνέομαι ‘refuse’, with στερεῶς ‘firmly’. ἐπὶ δ’ … ὄμοσσεν is the verb ἐπόμνυμι ‘swear in addition, swear to it’ in tmesis, and ὅρκον ‘oath’ is its object. The colon opens the oath.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὰ Ζῆν’, ὅς τίς τε θεῶν ὕπατος καὶ ἄριστος,
οὐ θέμις ἐστὶ λοετρὰ καρήατος ἆσσον ἱκέσθαι
πρίν γ’ ἐνὶ Πάτροκλον θέμεναι πυρὶ σῆμά τε χεῦαι
κείρασθαί τε κόμην, ἐπεὶ οὔ μ’ ἔτι δεύτερον ὧδε
ἵξετ’ ἄχος κραδίην ὄφρα ζωοῖσι μετείω.
sentences.tr:
ou ma Zēn’, hos tis te theōn hypatos kai aristos,
ou themis esti loetra karēatos asson hikesthai
prin g’ eni Patroklon themenai pyri sēma te cheuai
keirasthai te komēn, epei ou m’ eti deuteron hōde
hixet’ achos kradiēn ophra zōoisi meteiō.
sentences.l:
“No, by Zeus, who is highest and best of the gods,
it is not right for washing-water to come near my head
until I have placed Patroclus on the fire and heaped a mound
and cut my hair, since not a second time such grief
will come to my heart while I am among the living.
sentences.i: “No, by Zeus, who is the highest and best of the gods, it is not right for washing-water to come near my head until I have laid Patroclus on the fire, heaped a mound and cut my hair; for grief like this will not come to my heart a second time while I am among the living.
sentences.n: Achilles swears. οὐ μά with the accusative Ζῆν’ (Ζῆνα) is ‘no, by Zeus’, and ὅς τίς τε is ‘who’ in a general statement; ὕπατος is ‘highest’. λοετρά ‘washing-water’ is the subject of ἱκέσθαι ‘to come’, and καρήατος, the epic genitive of κάρη ‘head’, goes with ἆσσον ‘nearer’. οὐ θέμις ἐστί is ‘it is not right’. πρίν γ’ takes the infinitives θέμεναι ‘to place’ (aorist), χεῦαι ‘to heap up’ and κείρασθαι ‘to cut’, ‘until’ these are done. Cutting the hair was an offering for the dead; πυρί is ‘on the fire’, the pyre. ἐπεὶ οὔ … ἵξετ’ is ‘since … will not reach’ (ἵξεται, the future of ἵκω), with ἄχος ‘grief’ as subject and κραδίην ‘heart’ the object, and ὄφρα ζωοῖσι μετείω is ‘while I am among the living’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι νῦν μὲν στυγερῇ πειθώμεθα δαιτί·
sentences.tr: all’ ētoi nyn men stygerēi peithōmetha daiti·
sentences.l: But indeed for now let us obey the hateful feast;
sentences.i: But for now let us yield to the hateful feast;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι νῦν μέν is ‘but indeed for now’, set against ἠῶθεν ‘at dawn’ in the next line. πειθώμεθα is the subjunctive of exhortation of πείθομαι ‘obey, yield’, with the dative δαιτί, and στυγερῇ ‘hateful’ because he has no heart to eat.

sentences.t:
ἠῶθεν δ’ ὄτρυνον ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγάμεμνον
ὕλην τ’ ἀξέμεναι παρά τε σχεῖν ὅσσ’ ἐπιεικὲς
νεκρὸν ἔχοντα νέεσθαι ὑπὸ ζόφον ἠερόεντα,
sentences.tr:
ēōthen d’ otrynon anax andrōn Agamemnon
hylēn t’ axemenai para te schein hoss’ epieikes
nekron echonta neesthai hypo zophon ēeroenta,
sentences.i: and at dawn, Agamemnon, lord of men, urge them to bring wood and supply all that is fitting for a dead man to have with him as he goes down beneath the misty gloom,
sentences.n: ὄτρυνον is an imperative, ‘urge’, to Agamemnon (ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγάμεμνον is vocative), and the people he is to urge are named only at line 53. ἀξέμεναι ‘to bring’ and παρασχεῖν (παρά … σχεῖν) ‘to supply’ are infinitives; ὕλην is ‘wood’. ὅσσ’ ἐπιεικές is ‘as much as is fitting’, and νεκρὸν ἔχοντα νέεσθαι is ‘for a dead man to go having’. ζόφον ἠερόεντα is ‘the misty gloom’ of the underworld.

sentences.t:
ὄφρ’ ἤτοι τοῦτον μὲν ἐπιφλέγῃ ἀκάματον πῦρ
θᾶσσον ἀπ’ ὀφθαλμῶν, λαοὶ δ’ ἐπὶ ἔργα τράπωνται.
sentences.tr:
ophr’ ētoi touton men epiphlegēi akamaton pyr
thasson ap’ ophthalmōn, laoi d’ epi erga trapōntai.
sentences.l:
so that this man the untiring fire may burn up
the sooner from our eyes, and the people turn to their tasks.”
sentences.i: so that the untiring fire may burn him up the sooner out of our sight, and the people turn to their tasks.”
sentences.n: ὄφρ’ introduces a purpose clause with the subjunctives ἐπιφλέγῃ ‘burn up’ and τράπωνται ‘turn’ (aorist middle). τοῦτον is Patroclus, and ἀκάματον πῦρ ‘untiring fire’; ἀπ’ ὀφθαλμῶν is ‘from the eyes’, out of sight. λαοὶ … ἐπὶ ἔργα is ‘the people to their tasks’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα τοῦ μάλα μὲν κλύον ἠδὲ πίθοντο.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara tou mala men klyon ēde pithonto.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then readily heard him and obeyed.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they listened to him readily and obeyed.
sentences.n: A new paragraph. ὣς ἔφαθ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes Achilles’ speech, and the rest of the line has κλύον and πίθοντο, the imperfect of κλύω ‘hear’ and the aorist of πείθομαι ‘obey’. τοῦ is ‘him’, the epic genitive, and μάλα ‘readily’. The line stands in iliad-052 with the same English.

sentences.t:
ἐσσυμένως δ’ ἄρα δόρπον ἐφοπλίσσαντες ἕκαστοι
δαίνυντ’, οὐδέ τι θυμὸς ἐδεύετο δαιτὸς ἐΐσης.
sentences.tr:
essymenōs d’ ara dorpon ephoplissantes hekastoi
dainynt’, oude ti thymos edeueto daitos eïsēs.
sentences.l:
And eagerly then the supper having prepared, each company,
they feasted, and not at all did the heart lack the equal feast.
sentences.i: Eagerly each company got the supper ready, and they feasted, and their hearts went short of nothing in the equally shared feast.
sentences.n: ἐσσυμένως is ‘eagerly’, and ἐφοπλίσσαντες is the aorist participle ‘having made ready’, with δόρπον ‘supper’ and ἕκαστοι ‘each company’. δαίνυντ’ is ‘they feasted’ (δαίνυντο, imperfect), and οὐδέ τι θυμὸς ἐδεύετο is ‘nor did the heart lack at all’ (δεύομαι ‘lack’, with the genitive δαιτὸς ἐΐσης ‘the equal feast’, the meal shared fairly). Line 56 stands in iliad-005 in the same words.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
οἳ μὲν κακκείοντες ἔβαν κλισίην δὲ ἕκαστος,
sentences.tr:
autar epei posios kai edētyos ex eron hento,
hoi men kakkeiontes eban klisiēn de hekastos,
sentences.l:
But when of drink and of food they had put away desire,
those, then, went to lie down, each to his hut,
sentences.i: When they had put from them the desire for drink and food, the others, wishing to lie down, went each to his own hut,
sentences.n: πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος … ἔρον ἕντο is ‘put away desire of drink and of food’ (ἔρον the epic ‘desire’, ἕντο the aorist middle of ἵημι); line 57 stands in iliad-005 with the same English. οἳ μέν is ‘those, on the one hand’, the army, set against Achilles in the next line. κακκείοντες is ‘wishing to lie down’ (a future participle), and κλισίην δέ is ‘to a hut’, with the ending -δε ‘towards’.

sentences.t:
Πηλεΐδης δ’ ἐπὶ θινὶ πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης
κεῖτο βαρὺ στενάχων πολέσιν μετὰ Μυρμιδόνεσσιν
ἐν καθαρῷ, ὅθι κύματ’ ἐπ’ ἠϊόνος κλύζεσκον·
sentences.tr:
Pēleïdēs d’ epi thini polyphloisboio thalassēs
keito bary stenachōn polesin meta Myrmidonessin
en katharōi, hothi kymat’ ep’ ēïonos klyzeskon·
sentences.i: but the son of Peleus lay on the shore of the loud-roaring sea, groaning heavily among his many Myrmidons, in a clear place where the waves washed up on the beach;
sentences.n: Πηλεΐδης is Achilles; the lines tell where he lay, κεῖτο ‘was lying’, on the shore, ἐπὶ θινί. πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης is ‘of the loud-roaring sea’, and βαρὺ στενάχων is ‘groaning heavily’. ἐν καθαρῷ is ‘in a clean, clear place’, an open stretch of beach, and κλύζεσκον is an iterative imperfect of κλύζω ‘wash, dash’, so the waves kept washing there.

sentences.t:
εὖτε τὸν ὕπνος ἔμαρπτε λύων μελεδήματα θυμοῦ
νήδυμος ἀμφιχυθείς·
sentences.tr:
eute ton hypnos emarpte lyōn meledēmata thymou
nēdymos amphichytheis·
sentences.l:
When him sleep was seizing, loosing the cares of his heart,
sweet, poured round him;
sentences.i: As sleep took hold of him, loosing the cares of his heart, sweet and poured all about him;
sentences.n: εὖτε is ‘when’, and the sleep that seizes him (ἔμαρπτε, imperfect of μάρπτω ‘seize’) is νήδυμος ‘sweet’, a word whose meaning is not known; ‘sweet’ is the traditional sense. λύων μελεδήματα θυμοῦ is ‘loosing the cares of his heart’, and ἀμφιχυθείς ‘poured round’ is the aorist passive participle of ἀμφιχέω. The first line stands in odyssey-098 with the same English.

sentences.t:
μάλα γὰρ κάμε φαίδιμα γυῖα
Ἕκτορ’ ἐπαΐσσων προτὶ Ἴλιον ἠνεμόεσσαν·
sentences.tr:
mala gar kame phaidima guia
Hektor’ epaïssōn proti Ilion ēnemoessan·
sentences.l:
for greatly had grown weary his glorious limbs
rushing at Hector toward windy Ilios;
sentences.i: for his glorious limbs had grown very tired from rushing after Hector toward windy Ilios;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 63. κάμε is the aorist of κάμνω ‘grow weary’, with φαίδιμα γυῖα ‘glorious limbs’ as subject. ἐπαΐσσων ‘rushing at, charging’ takes Ἕκτορ’ (Ἕκτορα), the chase of Book 22, and προτὶ Ἴλιον ἠνεμόεσσαν is ‘toward windy Ilios’.

sentences.t:
ἦλθε δ’ ἐπὶ ψυχὴ Πατροκλῆος δειλοῖο
πάντ’ αὐτῷ μέγεθός τε καὶ ὄμματα κάλ’ ἐϊκυῖα
καὶ φωνήν, καὶ τοῖα περὶ χροῒ εἵματα ἕστο·
sentences.tr:
ēlthe d’ epi psychē Patroklēos deiloio
pant’ autōi megethos te kai ommata kal’ eïkuia
kai phōnēn, kai toia peri chroï heimata hesto·
sentences.i: and the soul of miserable Patroclus came to him, like Patroclus himself in everything: his size, his fine eyes and his voice, and wearing the same clothes about his skin;
sentences.n: ἦλθε δ’ ἐπί is ‘and there came up to him’, with ψυχή ‘soul’ as subject and Πατροκλῆος δειλοῖο ‘of miserable Patroclus’. πάντ’ αὐτῷ … ἐϊκυῖα is ‘like himself in all things’, the feminine perfect participle of ἔοικα ‘be like’, so the ghost looks as Patroclus did in life; μέγεθος ‘size’, ὄμματα ‘eyes’ and φωνήν ‘voice’ say in what. καὶ τοῖα … εἵματα ἕστο is ‘and such clothes he wore about his skin’ (ἕστο the pluperfect of ἕννυμι).

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.tr: stē d’ ar’ hyper kephalēs kai min pros mython eeipen·
sentences.l: and it stood then above his head, and to him spoke a word:
sentences.i: It stood over his head and spoke to him:
sentences.n: στῆ is the aorist of ἵστημι ‘stood’, ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς ‘above his head’, and μιν is ‘him’. πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν is ‘spoke a word to him’ (ἔειπεν the epic aorist of ‘say’). The colon opens the ghost’s speech. The line stands in odyssey-021 with ‘her’ for ‘him’.

sentences.t: εὕδεις, αὐτὰρ ἐμεῖο λελασμένος ἔπλευ Ἀχιλλεῦ.
sentences.tr: heudeis, autar emeio lelasmenos epleu Achilleu.
sentences.l: “You sleep, but of me forgetful you have been, Achilles.
sentences.i: “You sleep, Achilles, and have forgotten me.
sentences.n: The ghost of Patroclus is speaking. εὕδεις is ‘you sleep’ and λελασμένος (perfect participle of λανθάνομαι ‘forget’, with the genitive ἐμεῖο ‘of me’) means ‘having forgotten’. ἔπλευ is the epic ‘you have been, you are’ (a contracted aorist of πέλομαι).

sentences.t: οὐ μέν μευ ζώοντος ἀκήδεις, ἀλλὰ θανόντος·
sentences.tr: ou men meu zōontos akēdeis, alla thanontos·
sentences.l: Not indeed of me living were you neglectful, but of me dead;
sentences.i: You did not neglect me while I lived, but you do now that I am dead;
sentences.n: ἀκήδεις is the imperfect of ἀκηδέω ‘neglect, take no care’. The two genitive participles ζώοντος ‘while I was living’ and θανόντος ‘now that I am dead’ go with μευ ‘of me’, and ἀκήδεις has to be understood again after ἀλλά.

sentences.t: θάπτέ με ὅττι τάχιστα πύλας Ἀΐδαο περήσω.
sentences.tr: thapte me hotti tachista pylas Aïdao perēsō.
sentences.l: Bury me as quickly as possible; I would pass the gates of Hades.
sentences.i: Bury me as quickly as you can, so that I may pass the gates of Hades.
sentences.n: θάπτε is the imperative ‘bury’ (printed θάπτέ, with an acute on the last syllable before the enclitic με ‘me’). ὅττι τάχιστα is ‘as quickly as possible’, and περήσω, a short-vowel subjunctive of περάω ‘pass through’, gives the purpose without a conjunction; πύλας Ἀΐδαο is ‘the gates of Hades’.

sentences.t:
τῆλέ με εἴργουσι ψυχαὶ εἴδωλα καμόντων,
οὐδέ μέ πω μίσγεσθαι ὑπὲρ ποταμοῖο ἐῶσιν,
sentences.tr:
tēle me eirgousi psychai eidōla kamontōn,
oude me pō misgesthai hyper potamoio eōsin,
sentences.l:
Far off from me they keep me, the souls, phantoms of those who have toiled,
and not yet to join them beyond the river do they allow me,
sentences.i: The souls, the phantoms of those who have finished toiling, keep me far away, and do not yet let me join them beyond the river,
sentences.n: τῆλε is ‘far off’, and εἴργουσι ‘keep out’ has ψυχαί ‘souls’ as subject; εἴδωλα καμόντων is in apposition, ‘phantoms of those who have toiled’, the dead. The second line is ‘nor yet do they allow me (ἐῶσιν) to mingle (μίσγεσθαι) beyond the river’, the river that divides the dead from the unburied.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ αὔτως ἀλάλημαι ἀν’ εὐρυπυλὲς Ἄϊδος δῶ.
sentences.tr: all’ autōs alalēmai an’ eurypyles Aïdos dō.
sentences.l: but in vain I wander through the wide-gated house of Hades.
sentences.i: but I wander aimlessly through the wide-gated house of Hades.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ αὔτως is ‘but just so, to no purpose’, and ἀλάλημαι is the perfect of ἀλάομαι ‘wander’. εὐρυπυλές ‘wide-gated’ (εὐρύς ‘wide’, πύλη ‘gate’) agrees with δῶ, a shortened form of δῶμα ‘house’, and ἀν’ is ‘up and down, through’.

sentences.t:
καί μοι δὸς τὴν χεῖρ’· ὀλοφύρομαι, οὐ γὰρ ἔτ’ αὖτις
νίσομαι ἐξ Ἀΐδαο, ἐπήν με πυρὸς λελάχητε.
sentences.tr:
kai moi dos tēn cheir’· olophyromai, ou gar et’ autis
nisomai ex Aïdao, epēn me pyros lelachēte.
sentences.l:
And give me your hand; I grieve, for no more again
shall I come from Hades, when you have given me my share of the fire.
sentences.i: And give me your hand; I grieve, for I shall never come back from Hades again once you have given me my share of the fire.
sentences.n: δός is the imperative ‘give’, with τὴν χεῖρ’ ‘your hand’ (the article used as a possessive), and ὀλοφύρομαι is ‘I grieve’. νίσομαι is the present of νίσσομαι ‘go, come back’, with a future sense, and ἐπήν … λελάχητε is ‘when you have given me my share’, the reduplicated aorist of λαγχάνω used as a causative, with πυρός ‘of fire’; he means when the body has been burned.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν γὰρ ζωοί γε φίλων ἀπάνευθεν ἑταίρων
βουλὰς ἑζόμενοι βουλεύσομεν, ἀλλ’ ἐμὲ μὲν κὴρ
ἀμφέχανε στυγερή, ἥ περ λάχε γιγνόμενόν περ·
sentences.tr:
ou men gar zōoi ge philōn apaneuthen hetairōn
boulas hezomenoi bouleusomen, all’ eme men kēr
amphechane stygerē, hē per lache gignomenon per·
sentences.i: For never again, alive and apart from our dear companions, shall we sit down to take counsel together; the hateful death-spirit has gaped wide around me, the one that fell to me even at my birth;
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ is ‘for not indeed’, and ζωοί γε ‘alive, at least’; βουλὰς ἑζόμενοι βουλεύσομεν is ‘sitting we shall plan counsels’. κήρ is the death-spirit, and ἀμφέχανε ‘has gaped around’ means that it has swallowed him. ἥ περ λάχε is ‘which fell to me by lot’, and γιγνόμενόν περ ‘even as I was born’.

sentences.t:
καὶ δὲ σοὶ αὐτῷ μοῖρα, θεοῖς ἐπιείκελ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ,
τείχει ὕπο Τρώων εὐηφενέων ἀπολέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
kai de soi autōi moira, theois epieikel’ Achilleu,
teichei hypo Trōōn euēpheneōn apolesthai.
sentences.l:
and for you yourself too a portion is, resembling the gods, Achilles,
beneath the wall of the wealthy Trojans to perish.
sentences.i: and it is your fate too, Achilles, you who are like the gods, to perish beneath the wall of the wealthy Trojans.
sentences.n: καὶ δὲ … αὐτῷ is ‘and for you yourself too’, and μοῖρα ‘portion’ is the fate allotted, with ἀπολέσθαι ‘to perish’ (aorist middle infinitive) as its explaining infinitive. θεοῖς ἐπιείκελ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ is the vocative ‘Achilles, like the gods’. τείχει ὕπο has its preposition after the noun, ‘beneath the wall’, and εὐηφενέων ‘wealthy’ describes the Trojans.

sentences.t: ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω καὶ ἐφήσομαι αἴ κε πίθηαι·
sentences.tr: allo de toi ereō kai ephēsomai ai ke pithēai·
sentences.l: And another thing to you I shall say and charge, if you will obey:
sentences.i: And one thing more I shall tell you and lay on you, if you will obey:
sentences.n: ἄλλο δέ τοι is ‘and another thing to you’, and ἐρέω is ‘I shall say’. ἐφήσομαι is the future of ἐφίεμαι ‘enjoin, lay a charge on’, and αἴ κε πίθηαι is ‘if you will obey’ (πίθηαι, subjunctive of πείθομαι). The colon opens the request.

sentences.t:
μὴ ἐμὰ σῶν ἀπάνευθε τιθήμεναι ὀστέ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ,
ἀλλ’ ὁμοῦ ὡς ἐτράφημεν ἐν ὑμετέροισι δόμοισιν,
sentences.tr:
mē ema sōn apaneuthe tithēmenai oste’ Achilleu,
all’ homou hōs etraphēmen en hymeteroisi domoisin,
sentences.l:
do not my bones apart from yours lay, Achilles,
but together, as we were raised in your house,
sentences.i: do not lay my bones apart from yours, Achilles, but together, as we were brought up in your house,
sentences.n: μὴ … τιθήμεναι is the infinitive standing for a command, ‘do not lay’ (the epic ending -μεναι). ἐμὰ … ὀστέ’ is ‘my bones’, and σῶν ἀπάνευθε ‘apart from yours’. ὁμοῦ is ‘together’, and ἐτράφημεν is the aorist passive of τρέφω ‘be reared’; ὑμετέροισι is ‘your’ in the plural, the household of Peleus.

sentences.t:
εὖτέ με τυτθὸν ἐόντα Μενοίτιος ἐξ Ὀπόεντος
ἤγαγεν ὑμέτερόνδ’ ἀνδροκτασίης ὕπο λυγρῆς,
sentences.tr:
eute me tytthon eonta Menoitios ex Opoentos
ēgagen hymeterond’ androktasiēs hypo lygrēs,
sentences.l:
when me, little as I was, Menoetius from Opoeis
brought to your home, because of grievous man-slaying,
sentences.i: when Menoetius brought me, still little, from Opoeis to your home, because of a grievous man-slaying,
sentences.n: εὖτε is ‘when’, with τυτθὸν ἐόντα ‘being little’ agreeing with με. Μενοίτιος is Patroclus’ father, and Ὀπόεντος is the genitive of Opous, in Locris. ὑμέτερόνδ’ ‘to your (house)’ has the ending -δε, and ἀνδροκτασίης ὕπο λυγρῆς is ‘because of a grievous man-slaying’, a killing, with ὕπο after the noun.

sentences.t:
ἤματι τῷ ὅτε παῖδα κατέκτανον Ἀμφιδάμαντος
νήπιος οὐκ ἐθέλων ἀμφ’ ἀστραγάλοισι χολωθείς·
sentences.tr:
ēmati tōi hote paida katektanon Amphidamantos
nēpios ouk ethelōn amph’ astragaloisi cholōtheis·
sentences.l:
on the day when I killed the son of Amphidamas,
foolish, not wishing it, angered over knucklebones;
sentences.i: on the day I killed the son of Amphidamas, foolish as I was, not meaning to, in anger over a game of knucklebones;
sentences.n: ἤματι τῷ ὅτε is ‘on the day when’, and κατέκτανον is the aorist ‘I killed’. νήπιος ‘foolish’ and οὐκ ἐθέλων ‘not wishing’ both go with the speaker. ἀμφ’ ἀστραγάλοισι is ‘over knucklebones’, the game played with them, and χολωθείς ‘angered’ is an aorist passive participle.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά με δεξάμενος ἐν δώμασιν ἱππότα Πηλεὺς
ἔτραφέ τ’ ἐνδυκέως καὶ σὸν θεράποντ’ ὀνόμηνεν·
sentences.tr:
entha me dexamenos en dōmasin hippota Pēleus
etraphe t’ endykeōs kai son therapont’ onomēnen·
sentences.l:
there me, receiving in his halls, Peleus the horseman
reared with care, and your attendant named me;
sentences.i: There Peleus the horseman took me into his halls and brought me up kindly, and named me your attendant;
sentences.n: ἔνθα is ‘there’, in the house of Peleus. δεξάμενος ‘receiving’ is the aorist middle participle of δέχομαι, ἱππότα is the title ‘horseman’, and ἔτραφε is the aorist of τρέφω ‘rear’. ἐνδυκέως is ‘kindly’, and σὸν θεράποντ’ ὀνόμηνεν is ‘named me your attendant’, which is to say appointed me.

sentences.t:
ὣς δὲ καὶ ὀστέα νῶϊν ὁμὴ σορὸς ἀμφικαλύπτοι
χρύσεος ἀμφιφορεύς, τόν τοι πόρε πότνια μήτηρ.
sentences.tr:
hōs de kai ostea nōïn homē soros amphikalyptoi
chryseos amphiphoreus, ton toi pore potnia mētēr.
sentences.l:
so too may one coffin cover the bones of us two,
a golden amphora, which your lady mother gave you.”
sentences.i: so may one coffin cover the bones of us both, the golden jar that your lady mother gave you.”
sentences.n: ὣς δὲ καί is ‘and so too’, with the optative ἀμφικαλύπτοι ‘may it cover’, a wish. νῶϊν is the dual genitive ‘of us two’, and ὁμὴ σορός ‘one common coffin’. χρύσεος ἀμφιφορεύς is ‘a golden amphora’, a two-handled jar (‘jar’ in i), and πότνια μήτηρ ‘lady mother’ is Thetis. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: In answer Achilles, swift of foot, said to him:
sentences.n: A new paragraph, and Achilles replies. The line is the reply-formula τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη ‘answering him, addressed’, with πόδας ὠκύς ‘swift in feet’; the line stands in iliad-001 with the same English.

sentences.t:
τίπτέ μοι ἠθείη κεφαλὴ δεῦρ’ εἰλήλουθας
καί μοι ταῦτα ἕκαστ’ ἐπιτέλλεαι;
sentences.tr:
tipte moi ētheiē kephalē deur’ eilēlouthas
kai moi tauta hekast’ epitelleai;
sentences.l:
“Why, honoured head, to me have you come here
and each of these things enjoin on me?
sentences.i: “Why have you come here to me, honoured head, and charge me with each of these things?
sentences.n: Achilles answers. τίπτε is τί ποτε ‘why ever’, and εἰλήλουθας is the perfect of ἔρχομαι ‘you have come’. ἠθείη κεφαλή is ‘honoured head’, the head standing for the man; the sense of ἠθεῖος is not known, and ‘honoured’ is a guess. ἐπιτέλλεαι is ‘you enjoin’, a middle form with ταῦτα ἕκαστα ‘each of these things’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγώ τοι
πάντα μάλ’ ἐκτελέω καὶ πείσομαι ὡς σὺ κελεύεις.
sentences.tr:
autar egō toi
panta mal’ ekteleō kai peisomai hōs sy keleueis.
sentences.l:
but I to you
all things fully shall carry out and shall obey as you bid.
sentences.i: Yet I shall carry out everything for you in full, and obey as you bid.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 95. αὐτὰρ ἐγώ τοι is ‘but I, for you’, with the two futures ἐκτελέω ‘I shall carry out’ and πείσομαι ‘I shall obey’. πάντα μάλα is ‘everything fully’, and ὡς σὺ κελεύεις ‘as you bid’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μοι ἆσσον στῆθι· μίνυνθά περ ἀμφιβαλόντε
ἀλλήλους ὀλοοῖο τεταρπώμεσθα γόοιο.
sentences.tr:
alla moi asson stēthi· minyntha per amphibalonte
allēlous olooio tetarpōmestha gooio.
sentences.l:
But stand near me; for a little while, having thrown our arms around each other,
let us take our fill of baneful lament.”
sentences.i: But stand close to me; if only for a little while, let us throw our arms about each other and take our fill of baneful lament.”
sentences.n: ἆσσον στῆθι is ‘stand nearer’, with the imperative of ἵστημι. μίνυνθά περ is ‘even if only for a little while’, and ἀμφιβαλόντε is a dual aorist participle, ‘we two having thrown our arms around’, with ἀλλήλους ‘each other’. Line 98 repeats the second half of line 10, ὀλοοῖο τεταρπώμεσθα γόοιο, and its English is reused. The speech ends here.
